claims.claim: Retrieval is the process of bringing stored information back into conscious awareness; it is the third function of memory, after encoding and storage (OpenStax), the final stage after encoding and retention (APA), and the process of accessing stored information (Noba).
Psychologists name three forms of retrieval from long-term memory: recall, recognition, and relearning.
Recall is producing information from memory without cues, as in an essay test.
Recognition is identifying previously learned information upon encountering it again; it involves a process of comparison, as in a multiple-choice test.
Relearning is learning previously learned material again; faster relearning (savings) measures how much was retained, per the savings method.
A retrieval cue is a prompt or stimulus used to guide memory recall; cues work by association between present stimuli and stored experiences (e.g., a song evoking an old memory).
The encoding specificity principle holds that retrieval is optimal when retrieval conditions duplicate the conditions present when the memory was formed; it is attributed to Endel Tulving.

Context-dependent memory is the finding that memory improves when the surroundings at retrieval match the surroundings at learning (classic demonstration: divers recalling word lists better in the place where they learned them, Godden & Baddeley 1975, as described by Noba).
State-dependent memory is the condition in which memory for a past event improves when the person is in the same biological or psychological state as when the memory was initially formed.
The tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon is the experience of attempting to retrieve a specific name or word and failing, with the item usually eventually retrieved; it is a retrieval block, not a loss.
The ability to retrieve information from long-term memory is vital to everyday functioning, from basic self-care to driving to performing one's job.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is the tip-of-the-tongue feeling a sign of memory failure or a sign that the memory is intact?
positions: Popular framing treats not being able to produce a word as a failed memory.

APA Dictionary of Psychology describes the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon as a failed attempt to retrieve a specific name or word in which the item is usually eventually retrieved; OpenStax and Noba similarly treat retrieval difficulty as distinct from memory loss.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson follows the APA definition: the tip-of-the-tongue feeling is a temporary retrieval block, and the memory itself is usually intact. The lesson says so explicitly and does not present it as loss or damage.

positions: The APA Dictionary has a standalone entry for state-dependent memory but no standalone entry for context-dependent memory (its state-dependent entry cross-references context).
OpenStax 8.1 does not cover context dependence; the Noba Project covers it via the encoding specificity principle and the Godden & Baddeley (1975) diver study.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Context dependence is presented simply, sourced to the Noba Project (encoding specificity and the diver study), with the APA state-dependent entry covering the internal-state version. No unsupported depth is added.
